claims.text: The untreated baseline is an equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy with excellent high-temperature strength and poor room-temperature ductility.
Experimental irradiation resistance of untreated NbMoTaW has not been verified and is based on computational predictions.
The proposed intervention is to add less than 5 at% Ti to NbMoTaW during arc melting.
Homogenization near 1400 °C for several hours followed by aging at 600–800 °C will promote nanoscale Ti-rich precipitation.
The Ti-rich precipitates will be coherent and BCC.
The Ti-rich BCC precipitates will be uniformly dispersed throughout the NbMoTaW BCC matrix.
Minor Ti addition locally reduces stacking-fault energy in NbMoTaW.
The reduction in stacking-fault energy promotes heterogeneous nucleation of ductile precipitates.
The Ti-rich precipitates act as soft zones that facilitate room-temperature dislocation motion.
Second-phase precipitates can trap helium bubbles and thereby reduce helium damage in the surrounding matrix.
Coherent Ti-rich precipitates in NbMoTaW will serve as effective sinks for helium bubbles and other radiation-induced defects.
The precipitates will improve irradiation tolerance without compromising the intrinsic high-temperature BCC stability of NbMoTaW.
Ti-treated NbMoTaW will have greater room-temperature plastic strain capacity than untreated NbMoTaW.
Ti-treated NbMoTaW will exhibit less helium-bubble coalescence and lower irradiation-induced defect accumulation than untreated NbMoTaW.
Ti-treated NbMoTaW will retain high-temperature mechanical performance up to 1600 °C.
The anticipated benefits apply from room temperature through 1600 °C and under helium-ion irradiation conditions intended to simulate reactor environments.
Microstructural and phase stability must be controlled for refractory high-entropy alloys used at elevated temperatures.

The hypothesis is falsified if Ti-treated specimens show no statistically significant ductility improvement, degraded high-temperature performance, or no reduction in helium-induced damage relative to identically processed untreated controls.
